criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community water access conceptually and through two secondary published case studies (boreholes, surface ponds, and river water in Central Sudan; shallow and deep tube wells in rural Bangladesh).
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, the paper does not analyze any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or utility-governance mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulation). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, its analytical focus is likewise not a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor, but rather how social identity categories (gender, class, ethnicity, age, marital status) intersect with biophysical and hydrogeological materiality (soil/rock geology, seasonal rainfall, water table depth, and spatial/temporal heterogeneity of naturally occurring groundwater arsenic), with only passing background mentions of state/NGO tube-well installation and red/green arsenic well painting. Even if informal social norms were construed broadly under the plain wording, the paper still fails Criterion 3 (no empirical evidence), so plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Theoretical/conceptual feminist geography essay proposing four mechanisms (simultaneity, situated specificity, relationality, and fluidity) to incorporate ecological materiality into intersectionality theory. It contains no primary empirical data collection or analysis and is not a systematic empirical synthesis; its two case studies are narrative summaries of previously published research by Anne Coles (2005) and Farhana Sultana (2007, 2009, 2011). Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports no original or systematically synthesized empirical access outcomes, though the narrative summaries of secondary literature discuss gendered water-fetching labor, walking distance, seasonal water availability, and negotiated access to arsenic-free tube wells.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the article is a non-empirical theoretical essay without primary data or systematic review methods, there is no primary empirical study population/sample, rule-type exposure, or empirical study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with Spanish and Chinese translations of the abstract).

evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing on gender and water research, the article explores how intersectionality complicates the social dimensions of water access, use, and control.
In this article, I seek to push intersectionality forward by exploring how to better incorporate ecological dimensions as analytical concerns, with a particular focus on the materiality of water.

The first study examines how hydrogeological and seasonal variations impacted the social relationships around water access in Central Sudan in the 1960s. The second study examines the relationships between gender relations and arsenic contamination of tube wells in Bangladesh.

raw_response.exposure: Intersection of social relations (gender, ethnicity, class, age, marital status) with ecological and hydrogeological materiality (geology, seasonal rainfall, aquifer depth, and naturally occurring groundwater arsenic); no legal or administrative rule-type exposure
raw_response.outcome: No primary empirical outcome reported (secondary literature illustrations discuss gendered water collection responsibilities, source distance, seasonal availability, and access to safe vs. arsenic-contaminated tube wells)
raw_response.population_and_sample: No primary empirical sample (theoretical essay drawing on secondary published studies of 200 villages in Central Sudan from Coles 2005 and rural communities in Bangladesh from Sultana 2007, 2009, 2011)
raw_response.rationale: Exclude under E05 (No empirical evidence). This article is a theoretical feminist geography essay arguing that intersectionality theory should incorporate biophysical and ecological materiality alongside social categories. It presents no primary empirical data and no systematic synthesis methodology, relying instead on narrative summaries of two previously published studies (Coles 2005 on Sudan; Sultana 2007, 2009, 2011 on Bangladesh) to illustrate four theoretical concepts (simultaneity, situated specificity, relationality, and fluidity). It also lacks any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory exposure governing water access under Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Theoretical / conceptual essay with illustrative secondary case summaries (non-empirical)
